The DietView data model and input contract

Source: vignettes/data-model.Rmd
data-model.Rmd

This vignette shows how to describe your own table to DietView. DietView needs one thing from your data: one row per prey record, that is, one prey taxon found in one stomach. Taxonomy, tables, figures and dashboards are all built from that table and from a specification that says which column is which.

The example is the public ICES stomach-content extract that ships with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet).

library(DietView)

One row per prey record

Column names are free. You do not rename your data; you declare once which column plays which role. ices_diet is already in the long format DietView expects:

dim(ices_diet)
#> [1] 9639   28
names(ices_diet)
#>  [1] "stomach_id"        "prey_aphia_id"     "prey_name"        
#>  [4] "item_type"         "digestion_stage"   "digestion_label"  
#>  [7] "prey_count"        "prey_weight_g"     "prey_length_cm"   
#> [10] "haul_id"           "country"           "survey"           
#> [13] "year"              "month"             "quarter"          
#> [16] "lat"               "lon"               "ices_rectangle"   
#> [19] "depth_m"           "region"            "predator_aphia_id"
#> [22] "predator_latin"    "predator_common"   "n_fish_pooled"    
#> [25] "length_cm"         "weight_g"          "stomach_empty"    
#> [28] "regurgitated"

Prey columns come first (prey_aphia_id to prey_length_cm), then the haul and the predator, repeated on every record of the same stomach. The table has no kingdom to species columns. DietView adds them when you attach a taxonomy, here the frozen lineage ices_lineage (see the vignette on WoRMS).

Declaring roles with dv_spec() 

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",   # WoRMS AphiaID, used first when present
  prey_name      = "prey_name",       # scientific name, used when there is no ID
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)

The roles, what they do, and the ICES column that fills each one:

Role Required Purpose ICES column
predator yes the predator of each record; a grouping and display label predator_common
stomach yes the stomach each record came from; must be unique across the whole table, because stomach counts count distinct identifiers stomach_id
prey_id / prey_name at least one prey keys used to attach the taxonomy prey_aphia_id, prey_name
weight no the weight share (%W) prey_weight_g
count no number of individuals per record, for the numerical share (%N). Records without a count contribute nothing to %N, so unidentified material usually disappears from that view prey_count
digestion no enables the digestion diagnostic digestion_label
covariates no columns you want to compare diets across region, year, quarter
predator_latin no used to look up identification photos predator_latin

Columns you do not declare are kept and travel with the data: length_cm, country or ices_rectangle can be added as covariates later, or used to build new ones, such as length classes (see the dashboard vignette). For the digestion role we use the readable digestion_label rather than the code digestion_stage, because it also says where the stage was not recorded. Its labels are inferred from the older ICES format; check them against the ICES vocabulary before you rely on them.

What counts as a prey record 

table(ices_diet$item_type)
#> 
#>     non_food         prey unidentified 
#>           67         8019         1553

item_type sorts the records into three kinds. prey records carry a WoRMS AphiaID. unidentified records are food that could not be named; they have no AphiaID, and DietView keeps them as unidentified at every rank, which is the point of the package. non_food records are sand, stones, plastic and wood: real observations, but not diet, so they are dropped before the analysis.

Nematodes are a different case. They do have an AphiaID, but in fish stomachs they are mostly parasites of the fish rather than food. The lineage tells you which records they are:

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]
c(nematoda = sum(phylum %in% "Nematoda"), kept = nrow(dat))
#> nematoda     kept 
#>     1042     8530

Both choices belong to the analyst, which is why the data keep these records and the filter is written out in the code. Dropping them also removes 9 stomachs whose only records were nematodes or non-food items.

Empty stomachs live in ices_stomachs

A stomach with no prey has no prey record, so it has no row in ices_diet. The companion table ices_stomachs has one row per sampled stomach, empty or not:

st <- ices_stomachs
st$status <- ifelse(st$stomach_id %in% ices_diet$stomach_id, "with prey records",
             ifelse(st$stomach_empty %in% 1, "flagged empty", "no record, no flag"))
table(st$status)
#> 
#>      flagged empty no record, no flag  with prey records 
#>               1197               3458               4231
table(st$country, st$status)
#>     
#>      flagged empty no record, no flag with prey records
#>   BE            45                  2               195
#>   DE           117                 25               420
#>   DK           595                  7              1861
#>   NL           379                  0               586
#>   NO            61                 30                69
#>   SE             0               3394              1100

Of the 8,886 stomachs, 4,231 have at least one record and 1,197 are flagged empty. The other 3,458 have no record and no flag: almost all (3,394) are Swedish, and the Swedish data do not report the empty flag, so these stomachs are most likely empty, but the data do not say so.

This matters for every per-stomach measure. DietView counts the stomachs it sees, so the denominator of dv_fo_table() is the number of stomachs with at least one record: frequency of occurrence among feeding fish, not among all fish sampled. For cod, ices_stomachs holds 2,055 stomachs, while the prepared data below hold 991. Use ices_stomachs for the proportion of empty stomachs or the number of fish sampled per stratum.

Records and counts

A record is not an individual. prey_count gives the number of prey individuals behind each record, when it was reported:

c(records = nrow(dat), individuals = sum(dat$prey_count, na.rm = TRUE),
  no_count = sum(is.na(dat$prey_count)))
#>     records individuals    no_count 
#>        8530       10816        3468
tapply(is.na(dat$prey_count), dat$item_type, sum)
#>         prey unidentified 
#>         1952         1516

Declaring count lets you switch from shares of records to shares of individuals (%N). For cod, the two currencies at class rank:

cod  <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
t_rec <- dv_tree(prep_cod)
t_num <- suppressWarnings(dv_tree(prep_cod, currency = "numbers"))
by_rec <- t_rec[t_rec$rank == "Class", ]
by_num <- t_num[match(by_rec$id, t_num$id), ]
cmp <- data.frame(class = by_rec$label, parent = by_rec$parent,
                  records = round(by_rec$pct_occ, 1),
                  numbers = round(by_num$pct_occ, 1))
head(cmp[order(-cmp$records), ], 5)
#>           class              parent records numbers
#> 4  Malacostraca Animalia|Arthropoda    43.4    55.0
#> 7     Teleostei   Animalia|Chordata    27.1    25.9
#> 17           NA               NA|NA     8.3     0.7
#> 8            NA   Animalia|Chordata     6.6     3.0
#> 2    Polychaeta   Animalia|Annelida     6.2     4.9

Malacostraca rise from 43.4% of the records to 55.0% of the individuals, because 20% of the malacostracan records with a count hold more than one individual. The unidentified material falls out almost entirely: it rarely has a count, and records without a count contribute nothing to %N (dv_tree() warns, here about 461 cod records). The default currency is records for that reason.

Checking a table against a specification

dv_validate() stops if a declared column is missing, if there is no prey key column, or if a weight is negative. It warns about records with no prey key, weights that are not numbers and stomach IDs shared between predators, and it ends with a one-line description of the sample. It reports problems and never changes your data. It returns the data invisibly, so you can use it in a pipeline.

invisible(dv_validate(dat, spec))
#> 8530 records from 4222 stomachs of 22 predator(s); 2305 stomach(s) hold a single record; 531 record(s) lack a weight.

Mapping your own survey

To use DietView on another table, write a different dv_spec(). If your columns were sp, stom, aphia, wt_g and yr, you would write:

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator = "sp", stomach = "stom", prey_id = "aphia",
  weight = "wt_g", covariates = "yr"
)

The later steps (dv_prepare(), dv_build_tree(), dv_sunburst(), dv_build_html()) read the column names from the specification, never from your code. The article “Adapting DietView to your own survey” goes through the other choices you make with a new table.
